Key_Findings: Heptane droplets exhibited two-stage combustion: after the visible hot flame extinguished, a low-temperature 'cool flame' continued burning invisibly, consuming fuel and producing formaldehyde and carbon monoxide.
AI_Summary: Liquid fuels in space can keep burning with an invisible 'cool flame' even after a fire looks completely out, silently generating toxic gases.
Safety_Recommendations: Install multi-spectrum UV/IR and gas-phase CO/formaldehyde sensors rather than relying solely on visible-light smoke detectors.
Data_Quality_Note: Flame spread rate not applicable — FLEX measures droplet combustion lifetime and cool-flame duration, not spread along a surface. Min Ignition O2 is an illustrative threshold derived from published FLEX extinction limits.

Key_Findings: Large-scale 1-meter cotton-fiberglass sample burned rapidly in low-speed forced airflow, demonstrating that standard 1-g NASA-STD-6001 upward flame tests underestimate microgravity flame spread rates.
AI_Summary: Large fabric and composite surfaces burn faster in gentle spacecraft ventilation currents than ground tests predict.
Safety_Recommendations: Restrict exposed large-area textiles in high-airflow corridors and enforce automated ventilation shutoff on smoke alarm.
Data_Quality_Note: Flame spread rate sourced from Saffire-I mission summary (Urban et al., 2016). Min Ignition O2 is an illustrative value consistent with published Saffire flammability limits.

Key_Findings: Elevated oxygen levels (26.5% exploration atmosphere) significantly increased ignition propensity and toxic CO/HCN output during smoldering combustion of Nomex and Plexiglas samples.
AI_Summary: Future Moon and Mars habitats using higher oxygen levels face severe toxic gas hazards from smoldering plastics and fabrics.
Safety_Recommendations: Enforce strict material off-gassing limits and equip exploration cabins with rapid scrubbing systems for carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide.
Data_Quality_Note: Spread rate is an illustrative estimate consistent with smoldering regime reported in Saffire-VI summary. Min Ignition O2 is illustrative.

Experiment_Name: BRE (Burning Rate Emulator, part of ACME)
Key_Findings: BRE used a porous-sphere burner to emulate a burning solid in microgravity gaseous-fuel mode, measuring soot production rates and flame structure independent of fuel pyrolysis. BRE is a sub-investigation of the ACME package, not a solid-fuel test.
AI_Summary: The BRE burner lets scientists study flame soot and structure in microgravity without the complication of a melting fuel surface.
Safety_Recommendations: Design cabin air-quality sensors to detect soot precursors from both gaseous and condensed fuel combustion events.
Data_Quality_Note: Flame spread rate is not applicable — BRE is a gaseous burner experiment, not a surface spread test. Min Ignition O2 is illustrative. All numerical parameters are estimates derived from ACME/BRE published literature.

Key_Findings: Spherical diffusion flames in microgravity showed lower soot radiation losses, enabling stable combustion near extinction limits with minimal visible luminosity. ACME includes the BRE, s-FORTH, ACME-COLOR, and ECF sub-investigations.
AI_Summary: Gas leaks in microgravity can sustain nearly invisible flames at very low oxygen concentrations without visible rising heat plumes.
Safety_Recommendations: Use ultrasonic leak detectors and distributed catalytic gas sensors around all propulsion and life-support propellant lines.
Data_Quality_Note: Flame spread rate is not applicable — ACME measures diffusion flame extinction limits, not surface spread. Min Ignition O2 is an illustrative extinction-limit threshold from published ACME papers.

Key_Findings: Thin PMMA sheets self-extinguished in quiescent microgravity below 20% oxygen; flame spread rate was strongly dependent on sample width and airflow velocity rather than gravity level alone.
AI_Summary: Thin plastic sheets can self-extinguish in still microgravity air — but only if no ventilation is blowing across them. Airflow is the dominant driver, not gravity.
Safety_Recommendations: Store thin-film plastics (packaging, labels, bags) in sealed containers away from ventilation ducts; treat any loose film near a vent as a potential fire fuel source.
Data_Quality_Note: Spread rate is an illustrative order-of-magnitude value consistent with BASS published quiescent-flow results. Min Ignition O2 is from published BASS extinction data.

Experiment_Name: BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids II)
Key_Findings: Thick solid fuels require sustained external heat flux to maintain pyrolysis in microgravity and show narrow burning regimes near extinction; self-extinction can occur at low airflow but is not guaranteed across all fuel thicknesses and oxygen levels.
AI_Summary: Thick plastic components are harder to sustain burning in space — but self-extinction is not guaranteed, and NASA's guide notes this is a common misconception.
Safety_Recommendations: Use thick, high-density structural polymers where possible; do not rely on airflow reduction alone to suppress a fire — verify extinction with onboard gas analyzers.
Data_Quality_Note: Spread rate is an illustrative order-of-magnitude value consistent with BASS-II quiescent-flow results. Min Ignition O2 is illustrative.

Key_Findings: Extended cool-flame burning regimes were observed for heavy hydrocarbon surrogates, producing persistent aldehydes and peroxides without visible soot formation or bright flame.
AI_Summary: Heavy liquid fuels can undergo prolonged flameless oxidation in space, creating corrosive and toxic vapors without producing visible smoke.
Safety_Recommendations: Pair optical smoke alarms with chemical vapor sensors in payload racks handling liquid coolants or hydrocarbon fluids.
Data_Quality_Note: Flame spread rate is not applicable — CFI is a droplet combustion experiment. Min Ignition O2 is an illustrative cool-flame extinction threshold.

Key_Findings: Radiative heat feedback from nearby walls in narrow spacecraft racks accelerates flame spread and traps dense soot in confined volumes, raising both spread rate and toxic gas output compared to open configurations.
AI_Summary: Fires inside tight equipment racks heat surrounding walls and spread much faster than fires in open cabin areas.
Safety_Recommendations: Line avionics bays with non-combustible aerogel insulation and place aspirated smoke detectors directly inside rack exhaust ducts.
Data_Quality_Note: Spread rate and Min Ignition O2 are illustrative values consistent with the confined-rack combustion enhancement effect reported in ISS research literature.

Key_Findings: Confirmed cool-flame phenomenon across a wider droplet size range; CO2 suppression agents showed reduced effectiveness compared to Earth due to altered gas-phase transport in microgravity. Optimal suppression timing and dosing remain active research questions.
AI_Summary: Even the most common fire extinguisher gas (CO2) works differently in space — suppression strategies developed on Earth may not transfer directly to microgravity.
Safety_Recommendations: Design microgravity-specific suppression protocols and verify chemical extinction with onboard gas analyzers before declaring fire extinguished.
Data_Quality_Note: Flame spread rate is not applicable — FLEX-2 is a droplet experiment. Min Ignition O2 is illustrative. The '40% longer CO2 discharge' figure in earlier versions of this app was an invented specific — it has been removed.

Key_Findings: Nine different spacecraft materials tested; cotton-fiberglass composite showed highest spread rate while silicone-coated Nomex self-extinguished consistently, validating NASA-approved material selections for crew garments.
AI_Summary: Not all spacecraft-approved fabrics behave equally in space fires — some self-extinguish while others spread flames rapidly even in the same environment.
Safety_Recommendations: Preference silicone-coated Nomex and flame-barrier laminates over cotton composites for all crew-worn garments and soft goods in habitat interiors.
Data_Quality_Note: Spread rate is from Saffire-II mission summary (Urban et al., 2016). Min Ignition O2 is illustrative.

Key_Findings: Increasing forced airflow velocity from 10 to 20 cm/s doubled the flame spread rate, confirming that spacecraft ventilation systems are a primary driver of fire growth in microgravity.
AI_Summary: Doubling cabin ventilation speed approximately doubles how fast a fire spreads — the life-support fans keeping crew alive can rapidly escalate a fire emergency.
Safety_Recommendations: Integrate two-speed emergency fan mode in habitat design: normal operations at standard flow, automatic reduction on first smoke alarm to limit fire growth while maintaining crew oxygen supply.
Data_Quality_Note: Spread rate is from Saffire-III mission summary. Min Ignition O2 is illustrative. Note: Saffire-III flew on Cygnus OA-8, not OA-7.

Key_Findings: A 100% pure oxygen environment at 16.7 psi turned Velcro, nylon, and foam padding into explosive fuels, causing fatal cabin flashover within 17 seconds in a pre-launch pad test, not a microgravity event.
AI_Summary: Pure oxygen cabin atmospheres make ordinary materials explosively flammable, leaving virtually zero time for crew escape. This event drove all modern spacecraft atmosphere design.
Safety_Recommendations: This row is historical context only. See Tab 5 for the full narrative. NASA's response: mandated nitrogen-diluted mixed-gas atmospheres and standardized all materials testing under NASA-STD-6001.
Data_Quality_Note: This was a pre-launch ground test at 1g. No flame spread rate or Min Ignition O2 is applicable — these were not measured in the accident. Included for historical context only; excluded from the hazard ranking.

Key_Findings: A solid-fuel perchlorate oxygen candle spontaneously ignited during routine activation, burning for 14 minutes and filling the station with acrid smoke and toxic particulates, blocking one of two Soyuz escape routes.
AI_Summary: A routine oxygen candle turned into a 14-minute inferno that filled Mir with toxic smoke and blocked the emergency exit — revealing that chemical O2 generators are a severe fire hazard.
Safety_Recommendations: This row is historical context only. See Tab 5 for the full narrative. NASA's response: replaced chemical oxygen generators with electrolytic systems on the ISS and mandated two clear egress paths.
Data_Quality_Note: No quantitative spread rate or Min Ignition O2 applies to a chemical candle combustion event. Included for historical context only; excluded from the hazard ranking.

Key_Findings: A damaged Teflon-insulated wire inside oxygen tank 2 caused an electrical arc, igniting the insulation and rupturing the tank; the resulting explosion crippled the Service Module and forced use of the Lunar Module as a lifeboat.
AI_Summary: A manufacturing defect turned a routine stir command into a catastrophic explosion that cut power and oxygen mid-mission — crew survived only by improvising a lunar module lifeboat.
Safety_Recommendations: This row is historical context only. See Tab 5 for the full narrative. NASA's response: redesigned oxygen tanks with no internal wiring and added isolated backup life-support systems.
Data_Quality_Note: This was an explosion, not a fire with a measurable spread rate. No flame spread or Min Ignition O2 applies. Included for historical context only; excluded from the hazard ranking.
